And then you mention you felt happier when you weren’t dieting. This is merely you experiencing a form of cognitive dissonance over short term versus long term happiness. For example, today I had an intense craving for Oreos. I could have driven to the store, bought a pack and wolfed them down in my car, but I chose not to indulge my craving. True, if I had eaten the cookies, in the moment I would be happy, relishing the sweetness of my favorite treat and being washed away in the sensory experience of it all. But I knew that later, as I sat at my desk, totaling my calories for the day, I would severely regret my choices. I would love to live in a world where I could eat fries, donuts, and Oreos all day and still remain thin and healthy.

But I don’t, and I never will. It takes effort sometimes, navigating the urges that my body, designed for a time thousands of years ago, struggles with when placed in a world where mountains of food are available at the push of a button. I could give up, indulging in every craving the moment it appeared. I’d be happy at the moment.

But deep down, I wouldn’t be happy. I’d know, deep down, that it wasn’t natural, it wasn’t right, to live this way. What would I do with those feelings? I’d like to say I would get in shape again, use them for motivation. But if I was that far gone, it’s likely I’d deny them, twisting them around in my head and ignoring any logic thrown my way. Perhaps, for an outlet, I’d start a blog complaining about how society doesn’t cater to my ridiculous needs.

See? The sequence of events that leads one to participate in the FA movement is very clear.

Anyway, we move to our next example: How this toxic denial can twist any decision you make, no matter the outcome.

Maybe (and the odds are rather stacked on one side) you exaggerated the 13 pounds of weight loss.
